quote: [Aeneas saw] Neoptolemus in an orgy of killing
[Polites] vomited his life’s blood before their [Priam and Hecuba’s] eyes
[Priam told Pyrrhus that he had] defiled a father’s face with the murder of his son
There was no escape for Priam, death was now upon him
[Priam] buckled his armour long unused on shoulders trembling with age, girt on his feeble sword
[Priam] feebly threw his harmless spear
[Pyrrhus dragged Priam] his body trembling as it slithered through pools of his son’s blood
So ended the destiny of Priam … his mighty trunk lay upon the shore, the head hacked from the shoulders, a corpse without a name.
[Hecuba and her daughters] were sitting flocked around the altar, like doves driven down in a black storm … vainly embracing the images of the gods.
[where Hecuba and her daughters were sheltering] under the naked vault of heaven, there stood an ancient laurel tree, enfolding the household gods in its shade
The maiden daughter of Priam, Cassandra, dragged from her very sanctuary, with her hair streaming and burning eyes raised to heaven
[Cassandra’s] prophetic frenzy
The two serpents seized [Laocoon’s] two young sons … feeding on their helpless limbs
Entwined twice round his body and twice round his throat … his priestly ribbons befouled by gore and black venom … [Laocoon was] raising horrible cries to heaven
The two snakes escaped … making for the citadel of heartless Pallas
God had willed that these were lips Trojans would never believe
Rest, the most grateful gift of the gods
[The Greeks built the Trojan Horse] with the aid of the divine skill of Pallas Athene
The King of high Olympus does not allow it [Aeneas escaping with his wife Creusa]
[Sinon was] ready with all his Greek arts and stratagems
The trap was laid. These were the arts of the liar Sinon.
Listen now to this story of Greek treachery and from this one indictment, learn the ways of a whole people.
This was the cruellest thing I saw in all the sack of the city [losing Creusa]
Grief-stricken I called [Creusa’s] name … again and again, but there was no answer
We were swept along in the fighting, Iphitus and Pelias with me. Iphitus was no longer young and Pelias and been slowed by a wound
Rolling down on the heads of their enemies the gilded beams and richly ornamented ceilings of their ancestors.
No man could speak of such things [destruction of Troy] and not weep.
The last agony of Troy
Who could speak of such slaughter? Who could weep tears to match that suffering?
Everywhere there was fear and death in many forms.
Why do you choose to give yourself to such wild grief?
Wipe away the tears you are shedding for Creusa whom you loved
Three times her phantom melted in my arms, weightless as the wind
Greeks were cut down in their hour of triumph
I longed in my anger to avenge my country [by taking revenge on Helen] … how should Helen get to see her native Mycene?
O Queen, the sorrow you bid me bring to life is beyond all words
I shudder to remember
All the horrors I have seen, and in which I played a large part
Some hostile power confused me and robbed me of my wits [when Creusa disappeared]
Is this treachery or courage? Who would ask in dealing with an enemy?
I shall win praise for blotting out this evil [Helen] and exacting a punishment which is richly deserved
It is not the hated beauty of the Spartan woman … that is … laying low the topmost towers of Troy, nor is it Paris.
The clamour struck the golden stars
Down fell those fifty bedchambers, the so great hope of future generations, the doorposts proud with spoils and barbarian gold.
Guided by godheads not our own
We joined many battles, we fought through the blind night, and sent many Greeks down to Orcus.
Rage and anger drove my mind headlong, and it seemed to me a beautiful thing to die in arms.
Mindlessly I grabbed my weapons, and nor was there enough reason in arms.
Enough has been given to your country and to Priam: if Troy could have been defended by deeds of war, it would have been by mine.
Alas, what a sight he was! How changed from that Hector who returned wearing the spoils of Achilles and hurled Trojan fire at the ships of the Greeks!
Nor did your extreme devotion, Panthus, nor your knitted headband of Apollo protect you as you fell.
My spirit was restored to bring help to the king’s palace and to relieve our men with my support and to add strength to the conquered.
[Seeing the seizing of Cassandra] Coroebus threw himself into the column of men, intending to die.
